extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying discrete mathematics / relations
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and exercises about relations (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), closures, equivalence relations, partitions, congruence modulo m, and the basic definition of functions. Includes definitions, theorems, lemmas, worked examples, and many exercises asking for proofs or counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive (definition and reflexive closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is reflexive iff for every x in A, (x,x) ∈ R. The reflexive closure of R is the smallest superset of R that is reflexive; R is reflexive iff R equals its reflexive closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity relation i_A is always reflexive. Exercises: prove R is reflexive iff R is its own reflexive closure; show how reflexive closure interacts with other properties (e.g., if R is symmetric/transitive, what about its reflexive closure?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric (definition and symmetric closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is symmetric iff for all x,y, xRy implies yRx. The symmetric closure of R is the smallest symmetric superset of R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One way to form the symmetric closure is to include reverse pairs (intuitively R ∪ R^{-1}); exercises: if S is the symmetric closure of R, prove Dom(S) = Ran(S) = Dom(R) ∪ Ran(R). Also consider whether the symmetric closure preserves reflexivity/transitivity in given cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive (definition and transitive closure)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is transitive iff whenever xRy and yRz then xRz. The transitive closure of R is the smallest transitive superset of R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If S is the transitive closure of R, exercises ask to prove Dom(S) = Dom(R) and Ran(S) = Ran(R). Also study how transitive closure interacts with symmetry and antisymmetry (e.g., whether transitive closure of a symmetric relation remains symmetric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure as the smallest superset with property
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a property P (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), the P-closure of R is defined as the (if it exists) smallest subset S ⊆ A×A such that R ⊆ S and S has property P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct closures by considering the family F = {T ⊆ A×A | R ⊆ T and T has property P} and taking S = ⋂F (when nonempty). Exercises guide completing alternative proofs using this construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain/Range behavior under closures
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific statements about how domain and range change (or don't) when passing to closures: for symmetric closure S of R, Dom(S)=Ran(S)=Dom(R)∪Ran(R); for transitive closure S of R, Dom(S)=Dom(R) and Ran(S)=Ran(R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as exercises to prove; they give guidance on expected invariants under certain closure operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal vs smallest element in family under subset ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering sets of relations with a property (e.g., transitive closure yields C×C), one can ask for minimal elements of the family F under subset ordering and whether F has a smallest element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example exercise (bus company) asks to find a minimal element of F and to determine if F has a smallest element; emphasizes understanding of 'minimal' (no strictly smaller member) vs 'smallest' (subset of all members).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence relation on A is a relation R that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives examples (identity relation, congruence of triangles, same-birthday relation) and uses this definition as the basis for subsequent theorems about partitions and equivalence classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class and quotient A/R
rubrics_metrics.description: For an equivalence relation R on A and x∈A, the equivalence class [x]_R = {y ∈ A | y R x}. The set A/R = { [x]_R | x ∈ A } is the set of all equivalence classes (the quotient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation and interpretation: elements of A/R partition A. Exercises ask to identify classes in examples (e.g., same-birthday, x−y∈Z on ℝ) and to prove set equalities like P/B = {P_d | d ∈ D} in the birthday example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition (definition and relation to equivalence classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A family F ⊆ P(A) is a partition of A if (1) ⋃F = A, (2) F is pairwise disjoint (distinct members have empty intersection), and (3) every member of F is nonempty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem: If R is an equivalence relation on A then A/R is a partition of A (Theorem 4.6.4). Conversely, every partition determines an equivalence relation whose classes are the partition elements (Theorem 4.6.6). Exercises guide the proofs and lemmas used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation determined by a partition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a partition F of A, define R = ⋃_{X ∈ F} (X × X). Then R is an equivalence relation on A (the relation determined by F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemmas: R is reflexive (and indeed an equivalence relation), and for X∈F and x∈X, the equivalence class [x]_R = X. Use this construction to prove the bijection between partitions and equivalence relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic facts about equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: For an equivalence relation R on A: (1) x ∈ [x]; (2) y ∈ [x] iff [y] = [x]; (3) any two classes are either identical or disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 4.6.5 provides these facts and they are used to prove that A/R is a partition. Commentary in the text explains proving set equalities via mutual inclusion and using contrapositive where convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence modulo m as an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: For positive integer m, define x ≡ y (mod m) iff m | (x − y). The relation C_m = { (x,y) ∈ ℤ×ℤ | x ≡ y (mod m) } is an equivalence relation on ℤ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text checks transitivity explicitly and leaves reflexivity and symmetry to exercises; exercises ask for counting equivalence classes for C_2, C_3, and general m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation on ℝ by integer difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Define S = { (x,y) ∈ ℝ×ℝ | x − y ∈ ℤ }. This S is an equivalence relation whose classes are cosets x + ℤ = {..., x−2, x−1, x, x+1, x+2, ...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives example classes and points out classes are either identical or disjoint; shows how to reason about elements and names of the same class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of applying symmetric and transitive closures (symmetric-transitive closure matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain the symmetric transitive closure of R: let Q be the symmetric closure of R and S the transitive closure of Q. Alternatively let Q' be the transitive closure of R and S' the symmetric closure of Q'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims/exercises: S (transitive closure of symmetric closure) is the symmetric transitive closure of R; S' ⊆ S; it is not necessarily true that S' = S (exercise asks for proof or counterexample). This highlights noncommutativity of closure operations in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive closure preserves symmetry and transitivity (statements to prove)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S' is the reflexive closure of R then: (a) if R is symmetric, then S' is symmetric; (b) if R is transitive, then S' is transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are posed as exercises: adding the identity pairs (reflexive closure) does not destroy existing symmetry/transitivity; students are asked to give proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive closure of a symmetric relation remains symmetric (statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is symmetric and S is the transitive closure of R, then S is also symmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives a hint: show R ⊆ S^{-1} and S^{-1} is transitive, then use minimality of transitive closure to conclude S = S^{-1}. Exercise asks for formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antisymmetry may not be preserved when forming transitive closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Putative theorem considered: If R is reflexive and antisymmetric, the transitive closure S of R is a partial order. The naive proof 'we just add pairs to make it transitive so antisymmetry remains' can be incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are asked to evaluate the correctness of the proof, produce counterexamples or fixes, and identify proof strategies. This highlights that adding pairs to enforce transitivity can introduce pairs that violate antisymmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of a relation with an equivalence relation and induced quotient relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is compatible with an equivalence relation S iff for all x,y,x',y' in A, x S x' and y S y' imply (x R y) iff (x' R y'). If R is compatible with S, there exists a unique relation T on A/S such that [x]_S T [y]_S iff x R y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask to prove existence and uniqueness of T and conversely that if such a T exists then R is compatible with S. This is the standard criterion for passing relations to quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: From preorder to partial order via quotient
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is reflexive and transitive (a preorder) on A, define S = R ∩ R^{-1} (an equivalence relation). Then (a) S is an equivalence relation; (b) there is a unique relation T on A/S with [x]_S T [y]_S iff x R y; (c) T is a partial order on A/S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises guide the student to construct the quotient order and prove antisymmetry of T, giving the familiar passage from preorders to partial orders by collapsing mutually related elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function (definition as a relation with uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation f ⊆ A×B is a function from A to B (notation f: A → B) iff for every a ∈ A there is exactly one b ∈ B with (a,b) ∈ f (formalized as ∀a∈A ∃! b∈B (a,b)∈f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text includes examples and non-examples, explains value notation f(a) = b iff (a,b) ∈ f, and remarks that a function can be specified by a rule but need not be; exercises ask to check various relations for the function property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function value notation and specification by rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If f: A → B is a function and a ∈ A, the unique b with (a,b) ∈ f is denoted f(a). A function can be defined by a rule (e.g., g(x)=2x+3 for x∈ℤ), which implicitly defines the set of ordered pairs in the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate that the same formula may define different functions depending on domain (e.g., g: ℤ→ℝ vs h: ℝ→ℝ), and emphasize that any subset of A×B satisfying the definition is a function even if not given by a simple formula.
